title: Navigating with cd 🧭
description: Move between directories using absolute and relative paths. Master `.`, `..`, and `~`.

slides.title: The Change Directory Command 📂
slides.content:
## `cd` – Your Steering Wheel

`cd` (change directory) moves you to a different folder.

Syntax: `cd [directory]`

- If no directory is given, `cd` takes you home.
- `cd -` takes you to the previous directory you were in.

slides.title: Jump Home 🏠
slides.content: Go back to your home directory:

quizData.question: What does `cd ~` do?
quizData.explanation: `~` represents home, so `cd ~` (or just `cd`) takes you there.

slides.title: Absolute vs Relative Paths 🛣️
slides.content:
## Two Ways to Describe a Location

- **Absolute path**: starts from root (`/`). Example: `/home/alice/Documents`
- **Relative path**: starts from where you are now. Example: `Documents` (if you're already in `/home/alice`).

Relative paths use special symbols:
- `.`  – current directory
- `..` – parent directory (one level up)

quizData.question: If you are in /home/alice/Music, what command takes you to /home/alice?
quizData.explanation: `..` refers to the parent directory. `cd ..` goes up one level to `/home/alice`.

slides.title: Stay in the Current Dir 🧭
slides.content: `.` is useful for running scripts in your current location (e.g., `./script.sh`). But `cd .` does nothing – you stay put.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## The Dash Trick
`cd -` toggles between the last two directories. It's like a back button in your terminal!
